subject: science

promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Electric current as a flow of charge, measured in amperes
Resistance and how it affects current
Differences between series and parallel circuits
Static electricity: separating charge and forces between charges
Magnetism: poles, magnetic fields and the compass

questions.lo: Electric current as a flow of charge, measured in amperes
questions.q: What is an electric current, and what unit is it measured in?
options: A store of energy, measured in joules
A flow of electric charge, measured in amperes
A push from the cell, measured in volts
A flow of heat, measured in watts
questions.explain: An electric current is the flow of electric charge around a circuit, measured in amperes (amps, A).

questions.lo: Electric current as a flow of charge, measured in amperes
questions.q: Which instrument measures current, and how is it connected in a circuit?
options: A voltmeter, connected in parallel
A thermometer, connected in series
An ammeter, connected in series
An ammeter, connected in parallel
questions.explain: Current is measured with an ammeter, which is placed in series (in the loop) so all the charge flows through it.

questions.lo: Electric current as a flow of charge, measured in amperes
questions.q: A single loop circuit has a lamp. Where is the current largest?
options: It is largest just before the lamp and smaller after it
It is the same everywhere in the loop
It is largest at the negative terminal only
It is zero until it reaches the lamp
questions.explain: Current is not used up. In a single loop the same current flows at every point — the lamp transfers energy but does not reduce the current.

questions.lo: Electric current as a flow of charge, measured in amperes
questions.q: Conventional current is drawn flowing in which direction outside the cell?
options: From the negative terminal to the positive terminal
From the positive terminal to the negative terminal
In whichever direction the wires are longest
It does not have a fixed direction
questions.explain: By convention, current is drawn from the positive (+) terminal round to the negative (−) terminal. (Electrons actually drift the opposite way.)

questions.lo: Potential difference (voltage), measured in volts
questions.q: Potential difference (voltage) is measured in which unit?
options: Amperes
Ohms
Volts
Joules
questions.explain: Potential difference, or voltage, is the push that drives current round a circuit and is measured in volts (V).

questions.lo: Potential difference (voltage), measured in volts
questions.q: How is a voltmeter connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp?
options: In series, in the main loop
In parallel, across the lamp
Between the two terminals of the cell only
It does not need to be connected at all
questions.explain: A voltmeter is connected in parallel (across) the component to measure the potential difference across it.

questions.lo: Resistance and how it affects current
questions.q: What does resistance do in a circuit?
options: It stores energy for later use
It opposes the flow of current
It increases the voltage of the cell
It has no effect on the current
questions.explain: Resistance opposes the flow of current. It is measured in ohms (Ω).

questions.lo: Resistance and how it affects current
questions.q: A pupil increases the resistance in a circuit but keeps the same cell (same voltage). What happens to the current?
options: The current increases
The current decreases
The current stays exactly the same
The current reverses direction
questions.explain: For a fixed voltage, more resistance makes it harder for charge to flow, so the current gets smaller.

questions.lo: Differences between series and parallel circuits
questions.q: Which statement is true for a series circuit?
options: The components are on separate branches
All the components are in one single loop
Each component gets the full cell voltage
Removing one component leaves the others working
questions.explain: A series circuit has all components in one single loop with only one path for the current.

questions.lo: Differences between series and parallel circuits
questions.q: Two lamps are in series. One lamp is removed. What happens to the other lamp?
options: It gets brighter
It stays the same
It goes out, because the loop is broken
It keeps working on another branch
questions.explain: A series circuit is a single loop. Removing one lamp breaks the loop, so no current flows and the other lamp goes out too.

questions.lo: Differences between series and parallel circuits
questions.q: Why are the lights and sockets in a house wired in parallel rather than in series?
options: So they all switch off together
So each one gets the full mains voltage and can be switched on or off on its own
So the current is used up before it reaches the last one
Because parallel circuits use no electricity
questions.explain: In parallel each device gets the full voltage and works independently, so switching one off does not turn the others off.

questions.lo: Static electricity: separating charge and forces between charges
questions.q: When you rub two insulating materials together, how does one become charged?
options: New charge is created out of nothing
Electrons are transferred from one material to the other
Protons jump from one material to the other
The materials heat up and glow
questions.explain: Rubbing transfers electrons from one material to the other. This separates charge — it does not create new charge.

questions.lo: Static electricity: separating charge and forces between charges
questions.q: An object rubs against a cloth and gains extra electrons. What charge does the object now have?
options: Positive
Negative
No charge (neutral)
It depends on the colour of the cloth
questions.explain: Electrons are negative, so gaining electrons makes the object negatively charged. The cloth, having lost electrons, is left positive.

questions.lo: Static electricity: separating charge and forces between charges
questions.q: Two balloons are both given the same negative charge and brought close together. What happens?
options: They attract and stick together
They repel and push apart
Nothing, because charge only affects metal
They lose their charge instantly
questions.explain: Like charges repel. Both balloons are negative, so they push apart. Only opposite charges attract.

questions.lo: Magnetism: poles, magnetic fields and the compass
questions.q: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another?
options: They attract each other
They repel each other
Nothing happens
They join to make one bigger pole
questions.explain: Like poles repel. Two north poles (or two south poles) push apart; only unlike poles (N and S) attract.

questions.lo: Magnetism: poles, magnetic fields and the compass
questions.q: On a bar magnet, which way do the magnetic field lines point outside the magnet?
options: From south to north
From north to south
In a straight line only
They point inwards from all directions
questions.explain: Outside a magnet the field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. They are closest together, and the field is strongest, at the poles.

questions.lo: Magnetism: poles, magnetic fields and the compass
questions.q: Why does a compass needle point roughly north when left to settle?
options: It is attracted to the nearest wall
It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field
It always points towards the Sun
The needle is not magnetic at all
questions.explain: A compass contains a small free-turning magnet that lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, so its north end points roughly north.

questions.lo: Electromagnets and their uses
questions.q: How can you make a simple electromagnet stronger?
options: Use fewer turns of wire
Add more turns of wire, use a bigger current, or add an iron core
Disconnect the cell
Replace the iron core with plastic
questions.explain: An electromagnet is made stronger by adding more turns of wire, increasing the current, or using an iron core.

questions.lo: Electromagnets and their uses
questions.q: A scrapyard crane uses an electromagnet rather than a permanent bar magnet. What is the main advantage?
options: It needs no electricity to run
It can be switched on to lift metal and off to drop it
It attracts plastic and wood too
It works without any coil of wire
questions.explain: An electromagnet can be switched on and off, so the crane can pick up scrap and then drop it. A permanent magnet cannot be turned off.

questions.lo: Electromagnets and their uses
questions.q: Which of these devices uses an electromagnet?
options: A plastic ruler
An electric bell
A glass window
A wooden spoon
questions.explain: Electromagnets are used in electric bells, loudspeakers, motors, maglev trains and scrapyard cranes.
